---
title: "For Engineers & Researchers"
subtitle: "Back-of-envelope estimates before provisioning hardware."
---

MLSys·im produces quick, type-safe analytical estimates for capacity planning, hardware selection, cost modeling, and sustainability analysis, in seconds and from specifications alone. Equations are documented and tied to the relevant literature; hardware registry specs come from datasheets where available.

---

## Why Use Analytical Models

Before running expensive benchmarks or provisioning cloud instances, an engineer needs directional answers:

- **Will this model fit in GPU memory?** Check before renting the GPU
- **Why does training fail when inference fits?** Separate weights, gradients, optimizer state, and activations
- **What is the expected TTFT for my LLM?** Estimate before building the serving stack
- **How many replicas do I need for a P99 target?** Size serving capacity before benchmarking
- **What is the MoE routing tax?** Sweep expert imbalance before choosing EP topology
- **How many H100s do I actually need?** Model scaling efficiency before buying the cluster
- **What will this cost per year?** TCO analysis before signing the contract
- **How often will my training job crash?** Reliability modeling before committing to a 30-day run
- **What is the carbon footprint of this deployment?** Quantify before the sustainability review

MLSys·im answers these in microseconds using first-order equations. It does not replace profiling, but it shows *where to start profiling*.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Theory Behind the Tools
Each solver implements equations from the [Math Foundations](math.qmd) page. For the full conceptual framework, see the companion slide decks linked in the [Solver-to-Slides Map](#solver-to-slides-map) below.

## Quick Start: Roofline Analysis

The `Engine` implements the Roofline Performance Model ([Vol I · Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/11_hw_acceleration/11_hw_acceleration.html) · [Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_hw_acceleration_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-11), Williams et al. 2009) to classify workloads as compute-bound or memory-bound.

```{python}
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

# Single-node: Is ResNet-50 memory-bound on A100?
profile = Engine.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100,
    batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)
print(f"{profile.bottleneck}, {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"MFU: {profile.mfu:.1%}, Arithmetic Intensity: {profile.arithmetic_intensity:~.2f}")
```

The returned `PerformanceProfile` reports latency, throughput, bottleneck classification, Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU), arithmetic intensity, energy, and a feasibility flag, which together support a first-pass hardware assessment.

## LLM Serving Analysis

The `ServingModel` models the two-phase LLM inference lifecycle ([Vol I · Ch 13: Model Serving](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/13_model_serving/13_model_serving.html) · [Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_model_serving_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-13)): compute-bound prefill and memory-bound autoregressive decoding on a single device.

```{python}
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

serving = ServingModel()
fp16_res = serving.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=4096, batch_size=1, precision="fp16",
)
int4_res = serving.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=4096, batch_size=1, precision="int4",
)
print(f"FP16 on 1xH100 -> Feasible: {fp16_res.feasible} (Mem util: {fp16_res.memory_utilization:.0%})")
print(f"INT4 on 1xH100 -> Feasible: {int4_res.feasible} (Mem util: {int4_res.memory_utilization:.0%})")
print(f"INT4 TTFT: {int4_res.ttft.to('ms'):~.1f}, ITL: {int4_res.itl.to('ms'):~.2f}, KV-cache: {int4_res.kv_cache_size.to('GB'):~.2f}")
```

`ServingModel` immediately flags that unquantized FP16 `Llama-3.1-70B` exceeds a single 80 GB H100 (`Feasible: False`), whereas INT4 quantization fits comfortably on one H100 (or FP16 can be sharded across a multi-GPU node).

## Hardware Sweep Pattern

Compare devices programmatically instead of reading datasheets:

```{python}
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

model = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50

for hw in [mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
           mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100,
           mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.T4,
           mlsysim.Hardware.Edge.JetsonOrinNX]:
    p = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=hw, batch_size=32, precision="fp16")
    print(f"{hw.name:22s}  {p.bottleneck:10s}  {p.latency.to('ms'):>8.2f~}  {p.throughput.to('1/s').magnitude:>8.0f} img/s")
```

## Distributed Training Analysis

The `DistributedModel` models 4D parallelism ([Vol II · Ch 6: Distributed Training](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/06_distributed_training/06_distributed_training.html) · [Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_distributed_training_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-06)) with communication overhead from collective reductions ([Vol II · Ch 5: Collective Communication](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/05_collective_communication/05_collective_communication.html) · [Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_collective_communication_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-05)) and 1F1B pipeline bubbles.

```{python}
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel

dist = DistributedModel()
result = dist.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    batch_size=512, precision="fp16",
    tp_size=8, pp_size=4, microbatch_count=16
)
print(f"Scaling efficiency:  {result.scaling_efficiency:.1%}")
print(f"DP all-reduce:       {result.dp_communication_latency.to('ms'):~.1f}")
print(f"TP overhead:         {result.tp_communication_latency.to('ms'):~.1f}")
print(f"Pipeline bubble:     {result.bubble_fraction:.1%}")
print(f"Step latency:        {result.step_latency_total.to('ms'):~.1f}")
```

Tune `tp_size`, `pp_size`, and `microbatch_count` to find the parallelism configuration that maximizes scaling efficiency for a given cluster topology.

## Composing Solvers for Real Questions

The core solvers are designed to chain. Three common engineering workflows follow.

### Serving Llama-70B on H100s within budget

```{python}
import math
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import EconomicsModel, ServingCapacityModel
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet

# Step 1: Size INT4 H100 replicas for 40 QPS under a 2,500 ms P99 SLA
cap = ServingCapacityModel().solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    qps=40.0,
    target_p99_latency_ms=2500.0,
    max_seq_len=4096,
    mean_request_tokens=1024,
    output_tokens=256,
    precision="int4",
)

# Step 2: Pack replicas onto 8-GPU DGX H100 nodes and compute annual TCO
nodes_needed = math.ceil(cap.required_replicas / mlsysim.Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node)
serving_fleet = Fleet(
    name="Serving Pod",
    node=mlsysim.Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
    count=nodes_needed,
    fabric=mlsysim.Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR,
)
cost = EconomicsModel().solve(
    fleet=serving_fleet,
    duration_days=365,
    kwh_price=0.08,
)
print(f"Replicas needed: {cap.required_replicas} GPUs ({nodes_needed}x DGX H100 nodes)")
print(f"Annual TCO:      ${cost.tco_usd:,.0f} (CapEx ${cost.capex_usd:,.0f} + OpEx ${cost.total_opex_usd:,.0f})")
```

### Choosing a training region to minimize carbon

```{python}
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import SustainabilityModel

sustain = SustainabilityModel()
for grid in [mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec, mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg,
             mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland]:
    r = sustain.solve(
        fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
        duration_days=30,
        datacenter=grid
    )
    carbon_tons = r.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
    print(f"{grid.name:16s}  {carbon_tons:8.1f} tCO2e  "
          f"PUE={r.pue:.2f}  Water={r.water_usage_liters:,.0f} L")
```

For the theory behind PUE, WUE, carbon intensity, and the energy hierarchy, see [Vol II · Ch 15: Sustainable AI](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/15_sustainable_ai/15_sustainable_ai.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_sustainable_ai_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-15)).

### Reliability of a 30-day training run on 256 GPUs

```{python}
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ReliabilityModel

rel = ReliabilityModel()
result = rel.solve(
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    job_duration_hours=720,       # 30 days
    checkpoint_time_s=120.0       # 2 minutes per checkpoint
)
print(f"Fleet MTBF:              {result.fleet_mtbf.to('hour'):~.1f}")
print(f"P(failure before done):  {result.failure_probability:.1%}")
print(f"Optimal ckpt interval:   {result.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('minute'):~.1f}")
print(f"Expected failures:       {result.expected_failures:.1f}")
```

This solver implements the Young-Daly checkpoint model ([Vol II · Ch 7: Fault Tolerance](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/07_fault_tolerance/07_fault_tolerance.html) · [Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_fault_tolerance_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-07)), which sets the optimal checkpoint interval for long training jobs.

## Writing Custom Solvers

Subclass `ForwardModel` and return a frozen Pydantic result model to integrate cleanly with pipelines and differential explainers:

```python
import pint
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from mlsysim.hardware.types import HardwareNode
from mlsysim.solvers import ForwardModel

class PowerEfficiencyResult(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True, arbitrary_types_allowed=True)
    device: str
    flops_per_watt: pint.Quantity

class PowerEfficiencyModel(ForwardModel):
    def solve(self, hardware: HardwareNode) -> PowerEfficiencyResult:
        flops_per_watt = (hardware.compute.peak_flops / hardware.tdp).to("TFLOPs/s/kW")
        return PowerEfficiencyResult(device=hardware.name, flops_per_watt=flops_per_watt)
```

See [Writing a Custom Solver](solver-guide.qmd#writing-a-custom-solver) for the full guide.

## Type Safety

All quantities are `pint.Quantity` objects. Unit conversions are explicit, and dimensional errors are caught at runtime:

```{python}
#| echo: true
import mlsysim
hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
print(hw.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s"))
print(hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s"))
try:
    hw.memory.bandwidth.to("second")
except Exception as err:
    print(f"{type(err).__name__}: bytes per second can never become seconds")
```

Pint catches *physical*-dimension mismatches (bytes per second can never become
seconds). Since 2026-06, compute work also has its **own pint dimension**, so a
bare `.to("flop/s")` on a bandwidth raises `DimensionalityError` directly, as
does adding a FLOP rate to a memory bandwidth:

```{python}
#| echo: true
for label, attempt in [
    ("FLOP rate + bandwidth", lambda: hw.compute.peak_flops + hw.memory.bandwidth),
    ("bandwidth -> TFLOPs/s", lambda: hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TFLOPs/s")),
]:
    try:
        attempt()
        print(f"{label}: accepted (unexpected)")
    except Exception as err:
        print(f"{label}: {type(err).__name__}")
```

Bytes, counts, parameters, and dollars remain dimensionless aliases, so MLSys·im
additionally enforces **unit-family checks** at every schema boundary
(`require_unit_family` in `mlsysim.core.types`) to keep those distinct. A
field declared as memory bandwidth rejects a count rate, and vice versa.

Each MLSys·im solver maps to canonical chapters, interactive Marimo labs, and lecture decks in the [Machine Learning Systems](https://mlsysbook.ai) textbook (see the [Cross-Volume Textbook Map](curriculum-map.qmd) for all chapters and physics threads).

| MLSys·im Solver | What It Models | Textbook · Lab · Slides |
|:---------------|:---------------|:------------------------|
| `Engine` / `SingleNodeModel` | Roofline analysis, compute vs. memory bottleneck | [Vol I · Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/11_hw_acceleration/11_hw_acceleration.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_hw_acceleration_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-11)) |
| `CompressionModel` | Group quantization overhead, sparsity, accuracy delta | [Vol I · Ch 10: Model Compression](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/10_model_compression/10_model_compression.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_model_compression_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-10)) |
| `ServingModel` / `ServingCapacityModel` | TTFT, ITL, KV-cache memory, QPS/P99 replica sizing | [Vol I · Ch 13: Model Serving](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/13_model_serving/13_model_serving.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_model_serving_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-13)), [Vol II · Ch 10: Serving at Scale](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/10_inference/10_inference.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_inference_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-10)) |
| `DistributedModel` | 4D parallelism, all-reduce, 1F1B pipeline bubbles | [Vol II · Ch 6: Distributed Training](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/06_distributed_training/06_distributed_training.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_distributed_training_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-06)), [Vol II · Ch 5: Collective Communication](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/05_collective_communication/05_collective_communication.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_collective_communication_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-05)) |
